objectives: Explain why attention needs position information
Compare sinusoidal vs learned vs rotary encodings

slides.title: Part 1 — Attention is blind to order
slides.body: Attention's superpower — every token can see every other — comes with a flaw: it has no idea which token came first. Positional encoding is the fix, and the choice of *which* fix is one of the few architecture decisions that visibly changes a model's behavior at long context.

slides.title: The permutation-invariance problem
slides.body:
Attention is **permutation-invariant**. Shuffle the input tokens and it computes the same set of pairwise scores, just reordered. To raw attention, *"dog bites man"* and *"man bites dog"* are identical.

Fine for a bag of items; catastrophic for language, where order *is* meaning. We must inject position information into the inputs so attention can recover order.

The heatmap on the right shows the structured position signal we are about to build — each row is a position, each column a feature.

slides.title: Sinusoidal — the original recipe
slides.body:
The original transformer used fixed sine/cosine waves at geometrically-spaced frequencies:

$$PE_{pos,2i}=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right),\quad PE_{pos,2i+1}=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$

Every position gets a unique vector; nearby positions get similar vectors. This vector is **added** to the token embedding before layer 1. Because any offset is a linear combination of these sinusoids, the model *can* learn to attend "5 tokens back" with the right projection. Notice the banding in the viz: low dimensions oscillate fast, high dimensions slowly — a positional fingerprint.

question.question: Why does attention need positional encoding at all?
options: Attention is permutation-invariant — it sees every token pair but not their order
Attention cannot compute dot products without it
It is required for softmax to converge
question.explanation: Attention treats the input as a set: permuting inputs permutes outputs but doesn't change the computation. Order has to be injected into the inputs (added vectors) or into Q/K (RoPE) so the model can reason about sequence.

slides.title: Rotate, don't add
slides.body:
Every recent open model (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) uses **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)**. Instead of adding a position vector, RoPE *rotates* each Q and K vector by an angle proportional to its position. For a 2D slice:

$$\begin{bmatrix} q'_{2i}\\ q'_{2i+1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta_{p,i} & -\sin\theta_{p,i}\\ \sin\theta_{p,i} & \cos\theta_{p,i}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} q_{2i}\\ q_{2i+1}\end{bmatrix}$$

The key property: the dot product $q'\cdot k'$ between two rotated vectors depends **only on their relative offset**, not their absolute positions. *"the cat"* attends the same whether it's at the start or buried 900 tokens in.

slides.title: Why relative position is the right inductive bias
slides.body:
Language structure is mostly *relative*: a verb agrees with a subject some distance back; a closing bracket matches an opening one a few tokens prior. Absolute position ("token #347") is rarely what matters.

RoPE bakes relativity directly into the attention score, so the model never has to learn to subtract positions. It also **extrapolates** — ask for position 8000 after training on lengths up to 4000 and the rotation is still well-defined (especially with NTK-aware frequency scaling). A *learned* absolute embedding simply has no row for position 8000.

question.question: The main practical advantage of RoPE over learned absolute positional embeddings is:
options: It encodes RELATIVE position into Q·K and extrapolates to longer contexts than seen at training
It uses fewer parameters and is faster
It removes the need to train the model
question.explanation: Learned absolute embeddings memorize only the positions seen in training — position 8000 is undefined if you trained to 4000. RoPE's rotation is parametric in position and shows up as a relative offset in the dot product, so it generalizes far better to long context.

slides.title: Part 3 — Ablate it and watch it break
slides.body: The fastest way to internalize what a component buys you is to remove it.

slides.title: What happens with no positional encoding
slides.body:
Turn positional encoding fully off and train a small transformer:

1. **It collapses to bag-of-words.** Sentiment from word presence still works; syntax does not.
2. **Attention maps go uniform.** The diagonal/local-window structure vanishes.
3. **Generation degenerates.** Autoregressive sampling loops the same token — there's no notion of "what came before."

The loss plateaus far higher than the same model *with* PE. That gap is precisely the value positional encoding adds — a clean, runnable sanity check.

question.question: Order these positional schemes from OLDEST to NEWEST as the dominant default in transformer LLMs.
question.explanation: Sinusoidal came with the original 2017 transformer; learned absolute embeddings dominated the BERT/GPT-2 era; RoPE is the current default for modern LLMs because of its relative-position structure and extrapolation. (ALiBi is another modern relative-bias alternative.)

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- Attention is **permutation-invariant**; position must be injected.
- **Sinusoidal**: fixed waves added to embeddings — extrapolates, original recipe.
- **RoPE**: rotate Q/K so the score depends only on **relative** offset — the modern default, best long-context behavior.
- Remove PE and the model collapses to bag-of-words.

**Next:** [Attention](/wiki/attention) and [multi-head attention](/wiki/multi-head-attention) — now that each token's vector carries its position, attention can finally tell *"dog bites man"* from *"man bites dog"*.
